o: conversions forms a tree rooted at unit 0 where each edge (u, v, f) means 1 unit of u = f units of v. For a query (a, b) the answer is the rational ratio units(b per a) = w(a)/w(b), where w(u) is the product of edge factors along the root-to-u path. Working modulo 1e9+7, w(u) is computed by one BFS/DFS multiplying factors, and division becomes multiplication by the modular inverse (Fermat's little theorem, since the modulus is prime). Example 2: w(4) = 6*2 = 12 so (0,4) -> 12; (6,1) -> w(6)/w(1) = 24/2 = 12 -> inverse of 12 = 83333334.
k: Root the tree at 0; w(u) = product of factors from root, computed in one traversal.
Modular inverse via Fermat: pow(w, MOD-2, MOD), O(log MOD) per node.

a.i: BFS from unit 0 propagating w(child) = w(parent) * factor mod p. Each query is then a single multiplication with one modular exponentiation for the inverse.
s: BFS/DFS from 0 setting w[child] = w[parent] * f % MOD.
Answer each query as w[a] * pow(w[b], MOD-2, MOD) % MOD.
a.t: O(n log MOD + q) — one traversal plus one modular exponentiation per node for inverses
a.sp: O(n) for adjacency and the w array

w: Everything reduces to path products on a tree; the only subtlety is representing division as multiplication by a modular inverse. Factors up to 1e9 mean products must be reduced mod p at every step. Follow-up: batch the q inverses with prefix products to get O(n + q + log MOD) total exponentiations, or handle dynamic edge updates with link-cut trees.
